## Introduction

I picked this problem because it sits right at the intersection of "a
real institutional need" and "a genuinely hard multi-class classification
task": higher-education institutions have a direct interest in identifying
students at risk of dropping out early enough to actually intervene, not
just after the fact. I worked through this as a supervised multi-class
classification problem, using Kaggle's
[Playground Series S4E6](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/playground-series-s4e6)
dataset — a synthetic-augmented version of the UCI "Predict Students' Dropout
and Academic Success" dataset.

The task, as I framed it for myself: given a student's demographics,
socioeconomic background, admission record, and first/second-semester
curricular performance, predict whether they will ultimately be classified
as **Dropout**, **Enrolled** (still active, outcome pending), or
**Graduate**.

This writeup accompanies `notebooks/01_eda_and_modeling.ipynb`, which
contains the full exploratory and modeling code I ran. Here I focus on
*why* I took each step and what it revealed, rather than repeating every
line of code.

## Data

The dataset has one row per student and roughly three groups of features:

- **Demographics & background** — marital status, nationality, whether the
  student is displaced from their region, has educational special needs,
  is a debtor, etc.
- **Admission record** — application mode/order, course, previous
  qualification and its grade, admission grade.
- **Curricular performance** — units credited/enrolled/evaluated/approved
  and average grade, separately for the 1st and 2nd semester.
- **Macroeconomic context** — unemployment rate, inflation rate, and GDP at
  the time of enrollment.

### What "1st sem" / "2nd sem" actually cover, and why that's enough

The first thing I had to get straight before touching any code was what
the semester columns actually represent, because getting this wrong would
have quietly undermined everything downstream. Each semester field breaks
down as follows:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `credited` | Units credited without an exam (transfer credit, exemptions, prior qualifications) |
| `enrolled` | Units the student registered for that semester |
| `evaluations` | Number of evaluation instances (exams/assessments) undergone |
| `approved` | Units passed |
| `grade` | Average grade across that semester's evaluated units |
| `without evaluations` | Units enrolled in but never evaluated — disengagement, distinct from being evaluated *and* failing |

"1st sem"/"2nd sem" here means the student's **first academic year** —
Portuguese degree programs typically run 3+ years, and the target
(Dropout/Enrolled/Graduate) is recorded at the end of the program's normal
duration, years later. My first instinct was that predicting a multi-year
outcome from only the first year's data sounded like a limitation of this
dataset. On reflection I decided it's actually the point.

This reflects a real, well-studied use case: **early-warning dropout
prediction**. An institution doesn't want to wait until year 3 to notice a
student is at risk — by then it's often too late to intervene financially,
academically, or administratively. So the actionable question I kept coming
back to was: *using only what's known from admission plus the first year,
can at-risk students be flagged early enough to actually help them?* That
framing is also why I leaned so heavily on `approval_rate_1st_sem`/
`approval_rate_2nd_sem` and `grade_trend` as engineered features: a
student's *trajectory* within that first year (improving vs. declining,
engaged vs. disengaging) is a meaningful early signal for what happens over
the following years, even though the model never observes those later
years directly. The SHAP results below confirmed this for me empirically —
I didn't just assume it.

One thing I noticed early on: most "categorical" fields arrive as integer
codes (see the UCI documentation for the legend) rather than as strings —
a common data-cleaning trap, since a naive pipeline might treat them as
ordinal numeric features instead of unordered categories. It would be easy
to miss this and let a model quietly assume, say, that course code 9254 is
"between" 9253 and 9255, which means nothing. I made sure my preprocessing
pipeline (`src/academic_success/features.py`) explicitly one-hot encodes
them instead, so the model only ever sees "is this category present,"
never a false numeric order.

```{python}
#| label: fig-class-balance
#| fig-cap: "Target class distribution across the 76,518-row training set."
from academic_success import config, data

train_df = data.load_train()
counts = train_df[config.TARGET_COL].value_counts().reindex(config.TARGET_CLASSES)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.8))
bars = ax.bar(counts.index, counts.values, color=PALETTE[:3], width=0.6)
for bar, value in zip(bars, counts.values):
    ax.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2, value + 600, f"{value:,}\n({value / counts.sum():.0%})",
            ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=10)
ax.set_ylabel("Students")
ax.set_ylim(0, counts.max() * 1.22)
ax.set_title("Target class balance")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Why this matters
The classes are moderately imbalanced (~47% Graduate / 33% Dropout / 20%
Enrolled). That imbalance is exactly why I used macro-averaged F1 rather
than raw accuracy for every model comparison in this report: a model that
leans on the majority "Graduate" class would otherwise look deceptively
good on accuracy alone, and I wanted a number that couldn't hide a model
quietly ignoring the "Enrolled" class.
:::

## Feature Engineering

Beyond the raw columns, I derived a handful of features
(`src/academic_success/features.py`) that summarize a student's trajectory
across the two semesters rather than treating each semester in isolation.
The idea I kept testing against was: does this feature capture something
the raw columns can't?

- `approval_rate_1st_sem` / `approval_rate_2nd_sem` — the fraction of
  enrolled units a student actually passed, per semester. I added this
  because two students who both "enroll in 6 units" look identical on the
  raw columns, but one who passes all 6 and one who passes 1 are very
  different risk profiles — the approval *rate* captures that, the raw
  counts alone don't.
- `total_units_approved` / `total_units_enrolled` — cumulative load and
  success across both semesters, a coarser but more stable signal than
  either semester alone.
- `grade_trend` — the change in average grade from the 1st to the 2nd
  semester. A student improving over time is a different risk profile from
  one declining, even at the same average grade, and the raw per-semester
  grades alone don't tell you which direction someone is heading.
- `no_evaluation_ratio` — the fraction of a student's units that were never
  evaluated at all (as opposed to evaluated and failed). I treated this as
  a disengagement signal distinct from academic failure — a student who
  stops showing up to be evaluated is a different risk case from one who
  shows up and fails.
- `max_parental_qualification` — the higher of the mother's and father's
  qualification codes. **Caveat, stated plainly rather than glossed over:**
  these codes are categorical labels, not a ranked scale, so taking their
  numeric max is a common but imperfect Kaggle proxy for "at least one
  highly-coded parental qualification" — not a genuine ordinal measurement.
  I kept it because it's a widely-used trick on this kind of dataset, but I
  don't want to overstate what it actually measures.

One detail I almost missed and had to go back and fix: all ratio features
need to guard against division by zero explicitly (mapping `0/0` and `x/0`
to `0` rather than `NaN`/`inf`). It's a small, easy-to-miss data-cleaning
detail, but without it, every student with zero enrolled units in a
semester would have silently corrupted values flowing into the model.

```{python}
#| label: fig-approval-rate-by-outcome
#| fig-cap: "1st-semester approval rate by eventual outcome — the gap between Dropout and Graduate is exactly the signal this engineered feature was designed to expose."
from academic_success.features import FeatureEngineer

X_preview = train_df[config.RAW_FEATURE_COLS]
y_preview = train_df[config.TARGET_COL]
engineered_preview = FeatureEngineer().fit_transform(X_preview)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.8))
sns.boxplot(
    x=y_preview, y=engineered_preview["approval_rate_1st_sem"], hue=y_preview, legend=False,
    order=config.TARGET_CLASSES, palette=PALETTE[:3], ax=ax, width=0.5,
)
ax.set_xlabel("")
ax.set_ylabel("1st-sem approval rate")
ax.set_title("Approval rate cleanly separates the three outcomes")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

**Rare-category grouping.** When I looked at the categorical columns more
closely, several of them had a long tail of near-unique codes — I checked
the real training data and found `Father's occupation` has 56 distinct
codes, 44 of them below 1% frequency. That surprised me a bit; I hadn't
expected the tail to be *that* long. One-hot encoding all of them would
fragment the feature space into columns the model barely ever sees, and it
also risks an unseen rare code at inference time being treated identically
to *every other* unseen code by `OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")`'s
all-zero encoding — rather than being recognised as "the same kind of rare
code" the model saw examples of in training. To handle this I wrote
`RareCategoryGrouper`, which collapses any category below a frequency
threshold into a shared sentinel *before* one-hot encoding, learned from
training data only (no test-time leakage) — so a rare code the model has
never seen still gets grouped with other rare codes it has, instead of
being lumped in with common ones.

## Methodology

Here's how I put the pieces together, and why I made each choice rather
than defaulting to the first option that came to mind.

**Preprocessing.** Numeric features (raw + engineered) are median-imputed
then standardized; categorical (integer-coded, rare-grouped) features are
most-frequent-imputed then one-hot encoded, with unseen categories at
inference time mapped to an all-zero encoding rather than raising an error.
This means the pipeline won't crash if a course code shows up at inference
time that it never saw during training — it just treats it as "none of the
categories I know," which is safer than failing outright.

**Model selection.** Rather than assuming one model family would obviously
be best, I swept eight of them: a linear baseline (regularized logistic
regression), bagged trees (Random Forest), two classic boosting variants
(AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting), and four modern gradient-boosting
implementations (HistGradientBoosting, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) — see
`src/academic_success/model.py`'s `MODEL_FACTORIES`. I wanted the data,
not my instinct about which library is trendiest, to decide the winner.

**Class imbalance.** The target is moderately imbalanced (~47% Graduate,
33% Dropout, 20% Enrolled), so I evaluated ADASYN (Adaptive Synthetic
Sampling) as a possible mitigation. In plain terms, ADASYN manufactures
extra synthetic examples of the minority classes, concentrated in the
regions of feature space where the model finds them hardest to separate
from the majority class — the idea being that a model can't ignore a class
it's forced to see more of, especially near the decision boundary. I
implemented it via an `imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline` specifically so
resampling only ever touches the training fold — never validation or test
data, which would otherwise leak synthetic points into the score and make
the result look better than it really is.

**Ensembling.** I also evaluated a stacking ensemble (Random Forest +
XGBoost + LightGBM + CatBoost feeding a logistic regression meta-learner
via `sklearn.StackingClassifier`) against the best single model. In plain
terms, stacking trains several different models and then trains one more
small model whose only job is to learn how to weigh their predictions,
rather than averaging them with equal, fixed weight. I compared it on a
held-out split rather than nested cross-validation, because
`StackingClassifier` already runs its own internal 5-fold CV to generate
the meta-learner's training data — an *outer* 5-fold CV on top of that
would mean 25 fits per base model instead of 5, which felt like a poor
tradeoff of compute for the extra rigor it would buy.

**Interpretability.** I used SHAP (`shap.TreeExplainer`) to attribute
individual predictions to feature contributions for the final tree-based
model. My goal here was specifically to check whether the model actually
leaned on the trajectory features I'd engineered, or whether my
feature-engineering rationale was just a story I was telling myself.

**Validation.** All model comparisons use 5-fold cross-validation,
reporting both accuracy and macro-averaged F1 — I kept both numbers in
every table so the reader (and I) could double check that a high accuracy
wasn't secretly coming at the expense of the minority classes.

## Results

::: {.callout-tip}
## Where these numbers come from
The tables and charts below transcribe the actual output I got from
running `notebooks/01_eda_and_modeling.ipynb` Sections 9–12 against the
real downloaded competition data. I hard-coded them here rather than
recomputing them on every report render — re-running an 8-model x 5-fold
sweep plus a stacking ensemble just to render a report would take several
minutes for no new information, since the notebook is the source of truth
for these numbers.
:::

### Model sweep

I ran this on a stratified 15,000-row subsample with 5-fold CV, for fast
iteration (see Section 9 of the notebook) — using the full dataset for
every candidate model up front would have made this sweep far slower for
comparisons I mostly just needed a directional read on:

```{python}
#| label: fig-model-sweep
#| fig-cap: "Cross-validated macro-F1 across all 8 model families (15,000-row subsample)."
sweep_results = pd.DataFrame([
    {"model": "Gradient Boosting", "accuracy": 0.8247, "f1_macro": 0.7846},
    {"model": "HistGradientBoosting", "accuracy": 0.8230, "f1_macro": 0.7839},
    {"model": "Logistic Regression", "accuracy": 0.8229, "f1_macro": 0.7806},
    {"model": "LightGBM", "accuracy": 0.8197, "f1_macro": 0.7790},
    {"model": "CatBoost", "accuracy": 0.8198, "f1_macro": 0.7783},
    {"model": "Random Forest", "accuracy": 0.8191, "f1_macro": 0.7770},
    {"model": "XGBoost", "accuracy": 0.8146, "f1_macro": 0.7727},
    {"model": "AdaBoost", "accuracy": 0.8133, "f1_macro": 0.7692},
]).sort_values("f1_macro")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
bars = ax.barh(sweep_results["model"], sweep_results["f1_macro"], color=PALETTE[0])
bars[-1].set_color(PALETTE[3])  # highlight the winner
ax.set_xlim(0.76, 0.79)
ax.set_xlabel("CV macro F1")
ax.set_title("Model sweep — Gradient Boosting edges out the field")
for bar, value in zip(bars, sweep_results["f1_macro"]):
    ax.text(value + 0.0006, bar.get_y() + bar.get_height() / 2, f"{value:.4f}", va="center", fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### Full-data final model

When I trained the project's saved default (HistGradientBoosting,
`models/model.joblib`) with 5-fold CV on the *full* 76,518-row training
set, it reached **0.8317 accuracy / 0.7949 macro-F1** — beating *every*
model in the 15,000-row sweep above, including the one that nominally
"won" it on the smaller subsample. That's a bigger jump than I expected
from just adding more rows, and it changed how I thought about where to
spend effort next.

::: {.callout-important}
## Data volume beat model choice
This told me more training data mattered more than which model family I
used, at least within the model families I tried here. It's a common —
and easy-to-miss — result: it's tempting to spend effort tuning or
switching models when spending it on getting more (or better-utilized)
data would pay off more. I don't take this as a universal rule, but it's
exactly the kind of thing I wouldn't have caught if I hadn't measured the
full-data run separately from the subsample sweep.
:::

### Class imbalance: does ADASYN help?

I evaluated this on the sweep's best model (Gradient Boosting, same
15,000-row subsample), because I wanted to test the oversampling idea
against a model that was already doing reasonably well, not a weak one
that might make ADASYN look better than it really is:

```{python}
#| label: fig-adasyn-comparison
#| fig-cap: "ADASYN oversampling slightly hurt macro-F1 on this dataset."
resample_results = pd.DataFrame([
    {"resample": "None", "f1_macro": 0.7846},
    {"resample": "ADASYN", "f1_macro": 0.7829},
])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5))
bars = ax.bar(resample_results["resample"], resample_results["f1_macro"], color=[PALETTE[0], PALETTE[3]], width=0.5)
ax.set_ylim(0.77, 0.79)
ax.set_ylabel("CV macro F1")
ax.set_title("Resampling comparison")
for bar, value in zip(bars, resample_results["f1_macro"]):
    ax.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2, value + 0.0008, f"{value:.4f}", ha="center", fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

ADASYN moved macro-F1 from 0.7846 to 0.7829 — a small step *backward*,
not forward. I'll admit this wasn't the result I expected going in; I
assumed synthetic oversampling would help, since the classes aren't
perfectly balanced. What I take from this is that with only a moderate
imbalance like this dataset's, and a tree-based model already using
macro-F1 as the yardstick, there wasn't much headroom left for ADASYN to
recover — the extra synthetic points added noise without adding real
signal. That's a genuinely useful finding in its own right: it means the
project's saved model stays simpler than it would if I'd added ADASYN by
default.

### Ensembling: does stacking help?

I compared this on a held-out 20% split, same subsample, because I wanted
one more test of whether adding complexity (four base models plus a
meta-learner) was worth its cost over a single well-tuned model:

```{python}
#| label: fig-stacking-comparison
#| fig-cap: "The stacking ensemble roughly ties the best single model, at far higher training cost."
stacking_results = pd.DataFrame([
    {"model": "Best single model\n(Gradient Boosting)", "f1_macro": 0.7772},
    {"model": "Stacking ensemble", "f1_macro": 0.7742},
])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5))
bars = ax.bar(stacking_results["model"], stacking_results["f1_macro"], color=[PALETTE[4], PALETTE[3]], width=0.5)
ax.set_ylim(0.76, 0.79)
ax.set_ylabel("Holdout macro F1")
ax.set_title("Stacking vs. single model")
for bar, value in zip(bars, stacking_results["f1_macro"]):
    ax.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2, value + 0.0008, f"{value:.4f}", ha="center", fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Stacking landed at 0.7742 macro-F1 versus 0.7772 for the single Gradient
Boosting model — essentially a tie, and technically a very slight loss,
for four times the models to train and maintain. I went into this
half-expecting stacking to win by a clear margin, since combining models
is the textbook answer to "how do I squeeze out more performance." It
didn't, at least not here, and that's worth taking seriously rather than
writing off as a fluke of this particular split.

::: {.callout-important}
## Two negative results, reported honestly
Neither ADASYN nor stacking improved on the simpler alternative — ADASYN
made macro-F1 slightly *worse*, and stacking essentially tied the single
model while costing far more to train. Both surprised me a little going
in, and both are exactly why I kept the project's saved default model as
a single HistGradientBoostingClassifier rather than reaching for the
fancier options; see the Discussion below for why I think that's the
right call here.
:::

### Model interpretability (SHAP)

I ran this against the HistGradientBoosting final model, on a 500-row
sample, using the mean absolute SHAP value averaged across all 3 classes
— I wanted a single ranking I could sanity-check against the
feature-engineering reasoning above, rather than three separate
per-class rankings to eyeball:

```{python}
#| label: fig-shap-top-features
#| fig-cap: "Top 10 features by mean |SHAP value| — the engineered trajectory features dominate."
shap_results = pd.DataFrame([
    {"feature": "approval_rate_2nd_sem", "mean_abs_shap": 0.674},
    {"feature": "total_units_approved", "mean_abs_shap": 0.253},
    {"feature": "approval_rate_1st_sem", "mean_abs_shap": 0.180},
    {"feature": "Tuition fees up to date", "mean_abs_shap": 0.146},
    {"feature": "2nd-sem grade", "mean_abs_shap": 0.140},
    {"feature": "2nd-sem evaluations", "mean_abs_shap": 0.125},
    {"feature": "1st-sem grade", "mean_abs_shap": 0.099},
    {"feature": "Scholarship holder", "mean_abs_shap": 0.092},
    {"feature": "1st-sem evaluations", "mean_abs_shap": 0.084},
    {"feature": "Age at enrollment", "mean_abs_shap": 0.074},
]).sort_values("mean_abs_shap")

is_engineered = shap_results["feature"].str.contains("approval_rate|total_units")
colors = [PALETTE[3] if e else PALETTE[0] for e in is_engineered]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.8))
bars = ax.barh(shap_results["feature"], shap_results["mean_abs_shap"], color=colors)
ax.set_xlabel("Mean |SHAP value|")
ax.set_title("Engineered features (orange) dominate the top 3")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Discussion

Before I get to what the numbers mean, it's worth restating plainly what
SHAP actually is, since it does a lot of work in this section: it's a way
of taking a model's prediction for one specific student and splitting the
credit for that prediction across the individual features that produced
it, based on an idea borrowed from cooperative game theory (each feature
is treated as a "player" contributing to the prediction "payout"). The
practical upshot is a ranking of which features the model actually leans
on — not just which ones I *hoped* it would lean on.

Pulling the Results section's findings together: the engineered trajectory
features aren't just theoretically motivated (as I argued in Feature
Engineering) — SHAP confirmed they're what the model actually leans on
most, with `approval_rate_2nd_sem` alone outweighing the next-ranked
feature by more than 2.5x. That result mattered to me because it closes
the loop between *why* I built a feature and *whether* the model actually
agreed it mattered — it would have been easy to convince myself the
features were good just because they were plausible, without checking.

The two negative results (ADASYN, stacking) are ones I want to sit with
rather than rationalize away. Both are standard "try this, it should
help" techniques, and I went in expecting at least one of them to pay
off — neither did, here. That's precisely why I kept a single
HistGradientBoostingClassifier as this project's saved default
(`models/model.joblib`) rather than reaching for the more sophisticated
options: added complexity earns its place only when it actually earns its
keep, and I left `scripts/train.py --stacking` / `--resample` available
for anyone who wants to re-check that conclusion on a different split or
at full data scale — including future-me.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Limitations
I want to be upfront about where this project's conclusions do and don't
generalize:

- This dataset is a Kaggle Playground competition — a synthetic-augmented
  version of the original UCI data. I wouldn't deploy this on a different
  institution's population without re-validating it first.
- The "Enrolled" class is inherently ambiguous — it means the student's
  final outcome (Dropout vs. Graduate) simply hasn't happened yet, not that
  the model has genuinely identified a third *type* of student. I think
  this is worth flagging because it's easy to read "Enrolled" as a
  meaningful category rather than a placeholder for "still pending."
- The ADASYN and stacking comparisons ran on a 15,000-row subsample (for
  tractable notebook runtime) and a single train/validation split
  respectively — both conclusions are directional findings from this run,
  not guaranteed to hold at full data scale or across different random
  splits. I'd want to re-check them at full scale before treating either
  as settled.
- I didn't run a fairness/bias audit across demographic subgroups (e.g.,
  nationality, gender) here; a real deployment for an at-risk-student
  early-warning system would need one before use, since a model that's
  accurate on average could still be systematically wrong for a specific
  subgroup.
:::

## Conclusion

Looking back at the whole project, what I think made the biggest
difference was a moderate amount of feature engineering focused on
*trajectory* rather than snapshot performance — and, importantly, actually
validating that reasoning after the fact with SHAP rather than just
assuming it was right. Combined with a standard gradient-boosted tree
model, proper cross-validation, and an honest evaluation of fancier
techniques (ADASYN, stacking) that turned out not to help here, that was
enough to build a competitive, well-understood baseline for this task —
while staying at a scope I think is appropriate for a learning/portfolio
project rather than a production system.
